name: Prussian army of Frederick II (1740-1763)

weightNotes.aggression: Frederick: 'I prefer the boldness of a general who would rather hazard a battle at the right time', and a purely defensive plan 'is useless' (General Principles of War, 1748/1753). He attacked larger armies repeatedly: Leuthen 33,000 against 66,000 (Leuthen page), Zorndorf, Kunersdorf, Torgau.
weightNotes.maneuver: Interior lines and fast marches: 274 km in 12 days before Leuthen (Leuthen page); Rossbach followed five days of manoeuvre (Rossbach page). Battles themselves were bloody and attritional, so not higher (Showalter).
weightNotes.flanking: The oblique order refused one wing and massed against the enemy's flank (Oblique order page); Leuthen's approach was screened behind low hills to hit the Austrian left; Seydlitz's cavalry decided Rossbach from the flank.
weightNotes.siegePreference: Frederick sought decision in the field; the siege of Prague was abandoned after Kolin (Kolin page), and siege warfare was a Prussian weakness (Duffy). Low.
weightNotes.reserveUse: Nearly everything was committed to the attack; at Kunersdorf the king fed exhausted battalions into repeated assaults until the army dissolved (Kunersdorf page). Low.
weightNotes.scouting: Hussar patrols mainly guarded against desertion (General Principles), and Daun achieved complete surprise with a pre-dawn attack at Hochkirch (Hochkirch page). Peacetime knowledge of the Silesian ground helped at Leuthen. Middling.
weightNotes.retreatThreshold: Share of the engaged force lost before it withdrew or broke. Kolin 1757: 13,733 of 34,000 lost (40%) before withdrawing (Kolin page). Hochkirch 1758: over 30% lost in a surprise attack and the army still withdrew in order (Hochkirch page). Torgau 1760: 16,670 lost (about a third) in a victory (Torgau page). Kunersdorf 1759: the army dissolved and only 3,000 of 48,000 stayed with the king that night (Kunersdorf page). Frederick: wounded officers and men 'would not leave their posts' (General Principles). 0.35.
weightNotes.combinedArms: Superb infantry fire and the cavalry under Seydlitz as a shock arm (Rossbach, Zorndorf), with heavy guns added after 1757 (167 cannon at Leuthen). The arms fought in sequence more than in mutual support. Middling.
weightNotes.initiative: Frederick: 'everything that happens is the work of a single person' and 'no one talks, but all act, and the command of the general is promptly followed' (General Principles). Seydlitz's independent charges are the exception. Low.
weightNotes.logisticsDiscipline: Magazine-based: troops must 'want for nothing, be it meat, bread, straw', one can undertake everything 'if one only has enough food', and 'all wars in which we move too far from our borders are useless' (General Principles). High.

summary: A drilled long-service army, half native cantonists and half foreign recruits held together by severe discipline, fighting in thin lines with the fastest musketry in Europe. Frederick sought short, decisive campaigns on interior lines: quick marches, an attack on the enemy flank in oblique order with one wing refused, and heavy cavalry under Seydlitz to finish. Operations were tied to magazines close to the frontiers, and command was centralised in the king.
whyItWorked: Drill gave manoeuvre speed and fire rate no opponent matched, so a smaller Prussian army could concentrate on one enemy flank: Rossbach (1757, 22,000 beat 41,000 in about 90 minutes) and Leuthen (1757, 33,000 beat 66,000). Interior lines let Prussia fight Austria, Russia and France in turn, and the army's ability to absorb 30-40% losses and re-form kept it in the war for seven years.
whereItFailed: Against larger, well-led armies that held strong positions or attacked first, the costs were ruinous: Kolin (1757, 40% lost), Hochkirch (1758, surprised at night), Kunersdorf (1759, the army temporarily dissolved). Centralised command meant detached corps under lesser generals were destroyed. By 1760-62 Prussia survived on attrition and the collapse of the enemy coalition, not on battlefield decision.

sources.title: Frederick II, General Principles of War (1748/1753), German History in Documents and Images
Showalter, The Wars of Frederick the Great (Longman, 1996)
Duffy, The Army of Frederick the Great (Emperor's Press, 1996)
